extracted.intended_audience: Creators and operators of algorithms (industry practitioners), policymakers, regulators, and civil society organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended practices for designing, testing, auditing, governing, and regulating algorithms to detect, mitigate, and remediate bias and discriminatory impacts. Targets both organizational operators (designers, engineers, product managers) and policymakers/regulators who shape oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify how nondiscrimination laws apply to digital algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress can clarify how these nondiscrimination laws apply to the types of grievances recently found in the digital space, since most of these laws were written before the advent of the internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative action should provide clearer guardrails triggered when algorithms contribute to legally recognizable harms; clarification will incentivize more thoughtful technical design that avoids models likely to trigger or exacerbate explicit discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operators must develop a bias impact statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the idea for an algorithm has been vetted against nondiscrimination laws, operators of algorithms should develop a bias impact statement, offered as a template of questions to guide design, implementation, and monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the bias impact statement as a self-regulatory practice to probe and avert potential biases; brainstorm initial assumptions about purpose prior to development; apply the statement to assess purpose, process, and production; establish a cross-functional and interdisciplinary team to create and implement it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic Impact Assessments (AIAs) should include multi-stakeholder review and remediation processes
rubrics_metrics.description: AI Now’s model framework: AIAs evaluate potential detrimental effects of an algorithm across multiple rounds of review from internal, external, and public audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust AIA assumes (1) post-review companies develop a list of potential harms with outside technical experts, (2) if bias appears, notice is given to impacted populations with a comment period, and (3) the process supports users’ right to challenge algorithmic decisions; AIAs supplement but do not replace forethought and ongoing oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine which automated decisions require special scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators should start with questions about whether there will be a possible negative or unintended outcome resulting from the algorithm, for whom, and the severity of consequences for affected groups if not detected/mitigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established legal protections around fair housing, employment, credit, criminal justice, and health care as starting points; constantly question legal, social, and economic effects and liabilities when deciding what to automate and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider user incentives and external recognition for fair outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Incentives should drive organizations to proactively address algorithmic bias; operators who create and deploy algorithms that generate fairer outcomes should be recognized by policymakers and consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward effective algorithmic hygiene (before, during, after deployment) with possible public-facing acknowledgement to encourage trust and adoption of best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage stakeholders early and throughout algorithm development
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder engagement should help programmers select inputs and outputs and improve algorithms; users understanding products better than designers is key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get users engaged early and continuously; involve civil society organizations to add ground-level experience and avoid escalating complaints only to press/regulators; consider creating advisory councils of civil society organizations to define scope and predict biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: What will the automated decision do?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question from the bias impact statement template prompting clear articulation of the algorithm’s action or decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the decision’s scope, downstream effects, and how that fits into existing processes before development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is the audience for the algorithm and who will be most affected by it?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question to identify target users and populations likely to be impacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map affected groups, particularly protected classes and vulnerable populations, and analyze differential impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do we have training data to make the correct predictions about the decision?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question assessing whether available data supports accurate prediction for the intended decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate data relevance, completeness, and representativeness for the decision context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the training data sufficiently diverse and reliable? What is the data lifecycle of the algorithm?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question about data diversity, reliability, and lifecycle processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider provenance, collection methods, maintenance, updates, and decay of data; ensure representativeness and data quality across lifecycle stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which groups are we worried about when it comes to training data errors, disparate treatment, and impact?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question to identify groups at risk from data errors, disparate treatment, or disparate impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize review and testing for those groups and track error metrics by subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: How will potential bias be detected?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question on detection mechanisms for bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify measurement approaches, metrics, monitoring systems, audit trails, and thresholds for flagging bias across inputs and outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: How and when will the algorithm be tested? Who will be the targets for testing?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question on testing protocols, timing, and test populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan pre-deployment testing, ongoing testing post-deployment, targeted subgroup tests, and incorporate external/third-party testing where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: What will be the threshold for measuring and correcting for bias in the algorithm, especially as it relates to protected groups?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question about quantitative/qualitative thresholds for intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define acceptable disparities, statistical measures, and concrete remediation steps when thresholds are exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: What are the operator incentives?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question prompting reflection on organizational incentives shaping algorithm development and deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether incentives align with fairness goals (e.g., profit, efficiency) and design governance to mitigate perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: What will we gain in the development of the algorithm?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question on benefits and goals the operator expects from building the algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate intended improvements, efficiencies, or capabilities and weigh them against potential harms and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: What are the potential bad outcomes and how will we know?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question to list and detect adverse outcomes from the algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate harms (legal, social, economic), define indicators and monitoring processes to detect them, and specify reporting channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: How open (e.g., in code or intent) will we make the design process of the algorithm to internal partners, clients, and customers?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question concerning transparency choices across stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide levels of transparency appropriate for stakeholders (code, models, objectives, performance) while balancing IP and privacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: What intervention will be taken if we predict that there might be bad outcomes associated with the development or deployment of the algorithm?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question asking for predefined interventions upon predicted harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify mitigation strategies, rollback procedures, human-in-the-loop interventions, and escalation paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: How are other stakeholders being engaged?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question on stakeholder engagement mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail consultation plans, feedback loops, civil-society participation, and channels for impacted users to raise concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: What’s the feedback loop for the algorithm for developers, internal partners and customers?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question about feedback mechanisms across constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish ongoing channels for performance data, user reports, and iterative improvements; ensure feedback is actionable and prioritized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there a role for civil society organizations in the design of the algorithm?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question about involving NGOs and advocacy groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider formal roles (advisory councils, consultation, participatory design) to surface ground-level impacts and foresee biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Has diversity been considered in the design and execution?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question on whether diversity was factored into team composition, data, and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess workforce diversity, representativeness in testing, inclusive product design, and steps to fill gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will the algorithm have implications for cultural groups and play out differently in cultural contexts?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question about cultural sensitivity and contextual variation in impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test across cultural contexts, account for differing norms and impacts, and adapt designs accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the design team representative enough to capture these nuances and predict the application of the algorithm within different cultural contexts? If not, what steps are being taken to make these scenarios more salient and understandable to designers?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question prompting assessment of team representativeness and compensatory steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If team lacks representativeness, bring in external experts, user representatives, and targeted testing to surface overlooked scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Given the algorithm’s purpose, is the training data sufficiently diverse?
rubrics_metrics.description: Reiteration of data sufficiency question focused on alignment between purpose and representativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure data covers the populations and cases relevant to the algorithm’s purpose; fill gaps with targeted collection or synthetic augmentation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are there statutory guardrails that companies should be reviewing to ensure that the algorithm is both legal and ethical?
rubrics_metrics.description: Design question about legal and ethical compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review sector-specific statutes and nondiscrimination laws; consult legal and compliance teams early and throughout development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity-in-design
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators should consider diversity within work teams, training data, and the level of cultural sensitivity within decision-making processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a diverse workforce, integrate inclusive product spaces, and practice 'diversity-in-design' with deliberate transparent actions to address cultural biases and stereotypes upfront; this reduces risk of systemic bias and litigious/embarrassing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias impact statement should be proportionate and supported by ongoing review for high-stakes algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: The bias impact statement should not be exhaustive; for algorithms with more at stake, ongoing review of execution should be factored into the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for disparate impacts that border on unethical, unfair, and unjust decision-making; use robust feedback loops and periodic reassessments to detect bias over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operators should regularly audit for bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular formal auditing of algorithms to check for bias is a best practice for detecting and mitigating bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audits should review input data and output decisions; third-party evaluators can provide independent insight; audits can be technical or observational (stakeholder-identified outcomes); expect an audit trail; combine technical audits with responses from developers, civil society, and impacted parties. Examples: Allegheny County AFST independent evaluation; Facebook civil rights audit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on cross-functional work teams and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should employ cross-functional teams (engineering, legal, marketing, strategy, communications) or external experts to mitigate blind spots in algorithm design and rollout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use collaborative teams for accountability and risk mitigation; partner with academics and civil society for transparency and broader perspectives; avoid closed loops that prevent auditing and public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase human involvement in the design and monitoring of algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Human judgment should complement automated decision-making, especially for edge cases and ongoing monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain human moderators for edge cases, hire adequate staff, and use humans to arbitrate conflicts between outcomes and stated goals; be mindful of privacy implications when humans access sensitive data during testing and monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory sandboxes and safe harbors can support innovation while managing risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should implement regulatory sandboxes and safe harbors to allow technology and rules to evolve together, giving temporary reprieves from regulation while maintaining oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sandboxes allow testing of new approaches with active oversight; safe harbors can specify activities that do not violate regulations to increase regulatory certainty; consider safe harbors for collection of sensitive personal information when used specifically for bias detection/mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve algorithmic literacy among consumers and impacted populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread algorithmic literacy is crucial so subjects of automated decisions understand how systems function and how to respond when bias affects them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators/operators should solicit feedback and educate the public; public agencies can raise literacy as part of their missions; informed users help spot bias and contribute to remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and plan for trade-offs and limitations in fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some decisions will be best served by algorithms while others require careful consideration; testing and review will identify and mitigate discriminatory outcomes, but equity may never be fully realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge inherent trade-offs (technical and legal) and prioritize mitigation, oversight, and transparency; use testing to surface trade-offs and inform policy or human-in-the-loop choices.
